cues.text: A Miraculous Birth Foretold
John's birth was announced by the angel Gabriel to his father, the priest Zechariah, while he was serving in the Jerusalem Temple.
The news seemed impossible: Zechariah's wife Elizabeth was already advanced in years and had long been childless.
Zechariah doubted the angel's word, and for this his own speech was taken from him — struck mute until the child was born.
When Mary , newly pregnant with Jesus, visited her cousin Elizabeth, the unborn John is recorded as having leapt in his mother's womb at Mary's greeting.
Elizabeth herself, filled with the Holy Spirit, cried out in recognition of the child Mary carried.
It was the very first, wordless recognition of the relationship between the Forerunner and the One he had been sent to announce — offered before either child had drawn breath outside the womb.
A Prophet's Naming
At John's circumcision, relatives assumed he would be named after his father.
Elizabeth insisted he be called John instead.
When the still-mute Zechariah confirmed this in writing, his own speech was restored at once.
He burst into prophecy, blessing God for raising up a Savior.
Of his own infant son, he declared that the child would be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to prepare his ways.
This canticle has been known ever since as the Benedictus , still prayed each morning in the Church's Liturgy of the Hours.
A Voice in the Wilderness
Scripture tells us only briefly that John grew up in the desert.
As an adult, he emerged preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins along the banks of the Jordan River .

He dressed in a rough garment of camel's hair and lived on locusts and wild honey — an appearance deliberately reminiscent of the ancient prophet Elijah, whom many of his contemporaries believed he might in some sense embody.
Crowds came from Jerusalem and the whole surrounding countryside to hear him and be baptized, confessing their sins.
John's preaching was blunt and uncompromising, and it spared no one.
He called the religious leaders a "brood of vipers," and eventually he confronted the ruling king himself.
"I Must Decrease"
When Jesus himself came to be baptized, John recognized him immediately and protested.
He insisted their roles ought to be reversed, that it was he who needed baptism from Jesus rather than the other way around.
He yielded only when Jesus insisted it was fitting, for the moment, to fulfill all righteousness in this way.
John's own disciples later grew concerned as crowds increasingly followed Jesus rather than their own master.
John's response remains one of the most luminous statements of humility in the entire Gospel: he must increase, but I must decrease .
It is a forerunner's clear-eyed recognition that his entire mission existed only to point beyond himself.
Speaking Truth to a King
John's fearless preaching eventually turned to public rebuke of Herod Antipas , the regional ruler, for unlawfully taking his own brother's wife, Herodias, as his own.
This denunciation led to John's imprisonment.
Herod was troubled, and even fascinated, by John's preaching, but at first he did not dare kill a man so widely regarded by the people as a genuine prophet.
Herodias harbored a deeper grudge.
She found her opportunity at a lavish birthday banquet, when her daughter's dance so pleased Herod that he rashly swore to grant her any request.
Herodias exploited that promise through her daughter, demanding the immediate execution of John and the delivery of his head on a platter.
A Martyr's Death
Herod was trapped by his own public oath before his assembled guests.
Reluctantly, he ordered John's execution, and the great prophet who had baptized the Messiah himself was beheaded in prison.
Even from his cell, before this final act, John had continued to bear witness.
He sent his own disciples to ask Jesus directly whether he was indeed the one who was to come.
Jesus answered not with a simple yes, but by pointing to the very signs of the kingdom already unfolding around him — the blind seeing, the lame walking.
He entrusted John, even in doubt, with evidence rather than mere assertion.
Legacy
Christ's own assessment of John remains one of the highest tributes given to any human being in the Gospels: that among those born of women, none had arisen greater than John the Baptist.
He was the last and greatest of the Old Testament prophets, and the first to point directly at Christ as "the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world."
John stands at the exact hinge between two covenants.
His entire life and death were oriented, without reservation, toward preparing the way for someone greater than himself — a model of self-emptying witness the Church has never ceased to honor.
